title: A Perception Is a Meeting
reflection: Before one encounter that matters, settle the one wave you govern: three slow breaths for the rhythm, and a quiet release of the tilt, 'let me meet this, not defend against it'. Then notice whether the meeting itself changes.

questions.q: According to Conversation 3.2, what do you actually experience when you perceive something?
o: The world’s wave on its own, as it is, which your mind then colours afterwards with its own mood.
Your own wave alone, since the outer world is only a picture that your mind puts together in itself.
The world’s wave and your own wave added together: you live in the meeting, not in the bare world.
A copy of the world held in memory, which is replayed whenever you pay attention to something new.
questions.e: Swamiji’s image is two stones dropped in a pond. Each set of ripples carries on fully itself, the water adds them, and the criss-cross pattern belongs to neither stone alone. Every perception works this way: a wave from the world and a wave you bring, added.
questions.c: A perception is the meeting of two waves

questions.q: Dr Watson says two patients hear the identical sentence from him, one is reassured and one is wounded. How does Swamiji explain it?
o: One patient listened properly and the other did not, so the fault lies only with the one who was hurt.
The world’s wave was the same but their waves were different, so each lived a different meeting.
His tone must have changed between the two patients, though he cannot say how it came about.
One patient is simply more sensitive by nature, and nothing can be done to change how it lands.
questions.e: He did not hand them an experience; he offered a wave, and each met it with their own. Dr Watson takes from it that the news is never just the news. The content arrived both times; what changed was how each wave met it.

questions.q: “When two sets of ripples meet on a pond, they crash into each other and destroy one another’s pattern.”
questions.e: Swamiji’s point is the reverse: each set carries straight on, fully itself, and the water simply adds them at every point. Where two crests meet the water rises double; where a crest meets a trough the surface goes still. That pattern exists only in their meeting.
questions.c: Ripples add; they do not destroy each other

questions.q: James thinks of a pupil who ‘can’t do maths’ and whose wave is anxious and braced. What does the lesson suggest he does first?
o: Explain the material again more slowly and in more detail, since the pupil must be missing some content.
Close the gap first: meet the pupil’s rhythm and build a small success, so the same material streams whole.
Tell the pupil to try harder, because effort is what brings a wave closer to the rhythm of the lesson.
Move on to easier material for good, since the pupil’s capacity is plainly lower than the class’s.
questions.e: More content down a rough channel only arrives in more fragments. When the pupil’s wave is far from the material’s, there is a fast, rough beat. Shrink the gap and the very same material comes through whole: the moment pupils call getting it is the beat going quiet.
questions.c: Close the gap before adding content

questions.q: What does a piano tuner listen for, and what does it show about two waves?
o: The beat between the fork and the string: it slows as the two rhythms approach and vanishes when they match.
The loudness of the string, which grows greater as the string comes into line with the tuning fork.
The pitch of the fork alone, which she then copies as closely as she can by ear from memory.
The overtones above each note, which fade away the further apart the two rhythms happen to be.
questions.e: She listens to neither note but to the pulse between them. Far off pitch it is a rapid flutter; as the rhythms approach it slows; when they coincide it disappears and one full tone remains. In the mind, the beat is the gap between your wave and the world’s, made felt.
questions.c: The beat is the gap made audible

questions.q: “Even if your rhythm matches the world’s perfectly, arriving heavily tilted toward ‘what does this say about me?’ can still leave the meeting half empty.”
questions.e: Ahaṁkāra gives your wave a standing tilt before the meeting begins. The waves can be in tune and still not squarely face each other, so they do not fully add up; at the extreme they cancel, and someone present in body is absent in the meeting.
questions.c: A self-tilt empties the meeting even when tuned

questions.q: A friend says ‘I want to talk to you about something’ and Sarah braces at once. What does Swamiji suggest she does in that gap?
o: Take one slow breath and remember she is fundamentally fine here, so the tilt eases and she can listen.
Ask the friend straight away what she has done wrong, so that the worry can be settled at once.
Say nothing at all and wait for the friend to speak first, keeping her guard up until it is clear.
Change the subject to something light, so that the friend’s news does not arrive in a heavy way.
questions.e: The meeting is already tilted toward what this says about her, so even warm words must arrive through the brace. A breath and a quiet turn toward listening straightens the wave. Nothing changed in what the friend said; Sarah changed the angle she brought.
questions.c: Ease the brace with a breath, then listen

questions.q: Kai asks what shared medium lets the world’s wave and your wave meet at all. What is the answer?
o: The brain, since all experience must at last be carried out in nerve cells and their electrical signals.
Space and time, since every wave has to travel through them in order to arrive at the knower.
Consciousness itself: the world’s wave is it moving as the known, and yours is it moving as the knower.
Language, since a meeting of two waves needs a shared word before either of them can be noticed.
questions.e: Two sound waves can meet only because both move the same air; a sound wave and an ocean wave cannot meet. If experience really is a meeting, the two must be motions of one shared water. Nothing new is created in the meeting, so practice need only ease the misalignment.
questions.c: Both waves are motions of one Consciousness

questions.q: A patient is flooded: heart racing, spinning with worry, and cannot take in what Dr Watson says. What order does Swamiji endorse?
o: Body first, then meeting, then meaning: help the system settle, and then the insight can land.
Insight first, since the right understanding will calm the body once the patient has taken it in.
Argument first, since a patient who is shown the logic of the fear can then be talked out of it.
Waiting first, since nothing at all can be done for a flooded mind until the storm has gone by.
questions.e: An overdriven system makes its own weather and even manufactures rhythms that were never in either wave, so the patient cannot reason their way out. Slow breathing, less stimulation, steady rhythm and calm company lower the drive. Settling the water is often the healing itself.
questions.c: Settle the body first, then the insight can land

questions.q: In a conversation, Kai notices he has stopped listening and is waiting for his turn to speak. What is this, and what does he do?
o: The tilt arriving: he notes it, takes a breath and comes back to actually meeting the speaker.
A failure of manners, so he should resolve to speak far less in conversations from here onward.
A sign the speaker is dull, so he can fairly stop listening and think about what he will say.
A sign his wave is flat, so he should speak sooner, to put some life back into the exchange.
questions.e: This is Kai’s noticing practice: catch the moment the tilt arrives, take a breath and re-arrive. The aim is not to fix the other person but to see what he would otherwise have missed.
